newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraqi decries slow arrival of humanitarian food.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi decries slow arrival of humanitarian food.

text.p: Iraq's U.N. envoy complained on Monday to Secretary-General Kofi Annan over delays in the arrival of humanitarian goods under an "oil-for-food" deal that went into effect in December.

"We are today more than two months from ... the start (of the deal) and no kilo (2.2 pounds) of rice or sugar or whatever has really arrived in Iraq," ambassador Nizar Hamdoon told reporters after a meeting with the U.N. chief.
"They are expecting something to arrive in March. I only reflected on the frustration that we are having in Iraq on this operation," he added.

Under the "oil-for-food" agreement between Iraq and the United Nations, which entered into force on Dec. 10, Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian items to mitigate the effects of sanctions in force since Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Hamdoon said some contracts for food and other items had been approved by the U.N. sanctions committee, "but nothing has arrived in the country up till this minute."

He said the secretary-general promised "to do whatever is needed to speed things up." "I am not here to spread out accusations, but the whole process is very cumbersome and time-consuming," the Iraqi envoy said.
Hamdoon criticized what he said were delays within the U.N. sanctions committee, which must approve contracts for Iraqi purchases.
He said some of the food contracts were held up without explanation, which resulted in freezing the money from Iraqi oil sales earmarked for those purchases.
Asked about contracts for the sale of Iraqi oil, which have to be approved by U.N. overseers, he said: "We have not really encountered any difficulties."
